title: GPS: A Simple Way to Turn Goals Into Action
excerpt: I've always understood the importance of setting goals, but recently I came across a simple framework that changed the way I think about actually achieving them. The GPS Method — Goal, Plan, System — takes a goal and turns it into something much more practical: a destination, a route, and a way of keeping yourself moving.
content:
I've set plenty of goals over the years. Some were ambitious, some were fairly straightforward, and some probably sounded like good ideas at the time but never had much chance of surviving contact with real life.

That's the problem with a lot of goals. We're usually quite good at deciding what we *want*. The difficult bit is turning that decision into something we do consistently.

Recently I came across a simple framework called the GPS Method. I've only just started using it, so I'm certainly not claiming to have found the secret to achieving everything I want. What appealed to me was how simple it is. GPS stands for Goal, Plan and System, and the idea is that you need all three to turn an intention into something that happens.

The analogy is pretty straightforward. When you put a destination into a sat-nav, you've decided where you want to go: that's your goal. The sat-nav works out a route: that's your plan. But neither gets you anywhere unless you get in the car and drive, and that's the system. I think the driving is where a lot of goal-setting falls down.

## The destination

The first part is the obvious one: deciding what you want to achieve. Even here, though, we can make things harder than they need to be.

"I want to get healthier" isn't really a goal. Neither is "I want to become a better leader" or "I want to write more". Those are intentions. A useful goal needs enough definition that you can eventually look back and decide whether you achieved it.

I've also started to appreciate that the goal needs to mean something to you. It's very hard to keep up momentum towards something just because you think you *should* do it. Wanting to lose weight is one thing. Wanting to improve your health so you can stay active and enjoy more time with the people you care about is a very different proposition. The destination might be similar, but the reason gives it much more weight.

I like the idea of defining what you *don't* want to sacrifice along the way, too. These are sometimes called anti-goals. If I decide I want to get fitter, that doesn't mean I'm prepared to spend every evening in the gym. If I want to achieve something professionally, that doesn't mean I'm prepared to give up everything outside work. Knowing the boundaries of the journey matters as much as knowing where it ends.

## The route

Once you know where you're going, you need some idea of how you'll get there.

This is the part that stops goals becoming wishful thinking. Instead of just saying what you want, you identify the handful of things most likely to get you there. It doesn't need to be an enormous plan, and I think the simpler it is, the better. If the goal is getting fitter, the plan might be walking more, eating sensibly and training consistently. If the goal is developing as a leader, it might mean being more deliberate about one-to-ones, asking for feedback and spending more time reflecting on how you communicate.

The trick is finding the things that make a real difference, instead of filling your plan with activities that make you *feel* productive.

Then comes the reality check: would you actually do this? It's easy to write a brilliant plan when you're motivated. The real test is whether it still works when you're tired, busy, travelling, stressed or just can't be bothered. I've definitely been guilty of plans that looked great on paper but relied on me being motivated every single day. A slightly less ambitious plan I can follow consistently is far more useful than a perfect one that lasts two weeks.

One idea in the GPS Method is to imagine you've reached the end of your chosen period and haven't achieved the goal. What probably went wrong? Thinking about that in advance can expose weaknesses in the plan before they become problems.

## The bit that makes it happen

The final part is the system, and it's probably the bit I find most useful.

A goal gives you something to aim for and a plan tells you what to do. The system is what helps you keep doing it. That might mean tracking your progress, putting things in your calendar, setting reminders, using an app, having someone hold you accountable, or building routines that make the behaviour easier to repeat.

The point is that you're not relying entirely on motivation. Motivation is great when you have it, but it isn't reliable, and a system gives you something to fall back on when it disappears.

That's why tracking can be surprisingly powerful. Whether it's steps, workouts, money saved, words written or something else, seeing what you've done creates a feedback loop. You can tell whether the plan is working instead of going on how you *feel* about your progress, and when it isn't working, you can change it.

That's another reason I like the sat-nav analogy. A sat-nav doesn't treat a wrong turn as the end of the journey. It recalculates. I think personal development should probably work the same way. Missing a workout doesn't mean you've failed at getting fit, and a bad week doesn't mean the goal was wrong. Sometimes the plan just needs adjusting.

## Why I'm giving it a try

What I like about the GPS Method is that it doesn't pretend setting a goal is enough.

I've spent plenty of time thinking about things I wanted to change, and I suspect most people have. Knowing what we want is often the easy part. The hard part is turning it into consistent action while the rest of life carries on around us.

GPS gives me a simple way of thinking about that:

- Goal: where am I trying to get to, and why does it matter?
- Plan: what are the few things I need to do consistently to give myself a realistic chance of getting there?
- System: what can I put in place so that I keep doing those things?

It's early days, so I don't know yet how useful it will be over the long term. But I like that it doesn't need another complicated productivity system or hours of planning. You can sit down for ten minutes, work through the three stages and come away with something far more useful than a goal written on a piece of paper. And the part it puts the most weight on, the system that keeps you moving, is the part I've found hardest in the past.
